title: Chainsaw chain: filing, fitting, tensioning and the chain brake
summary: Keep a saw chain cutting with a round file of the right size, the right angle on every cutter, both sides equal and the depth gauges at the maker's height, then fit and tension it the right way round. A badly filed or loose chain makes kickback more likely and more violent, and kickback is how chainsaws hurt people.

steps.text: Stop the engine and put the chain brake on; take the battery out of a battery saw (STIHL MSA 60/70) or unplug a corded one (Oregon CS1500). On a petrol saw, pull the spark plug cap off too: Husqvarna's stop switch springs back to the start position, so a tug on the starter could fire the engine while your hands are on the chain (Husqvarna 450 II). Put on leather work gloves (Oregon sharpening, CCOHS chainsaw PPE).
steps.warn: A stopped chain still cuts (Husqvarna 450 II). Sharpen only with the engine off and the brake on (STIHL MS 162/172).

steps.text: Clamp the bar in a vice or stump vice and snug the chain up a little so the cutters don't rock as you file (STIHL UK sharpening). Release the brake only to pull the chain round, then set it again (STIHL MS 162/172, Oregon sharpening).

Find the pitch: STIHL stamps a number on each depth gauge (1 = 1/4 in, 2 = .325 in, 3 = 3/8 in, 4 = .404 in, 6 = 3/8 in Picco, 7 = 1/4 in Picco); Oregon prints a chain code on the drive links. Pick the round file for that pitch from the table in the notes (STIHL MS 162/172, STIHL UK sharpening, Oregon sharpening).

Look over the chain before you file. Replace it if a wear mark has gone, if the longest part of a cutting tooth is under 4 mm (0.16 in), or if cutters or links are cracked, rivets turn under your fingers, or links are stiff (STIHL MS 162/172, Husqvarna 450 II, Oregon sharpening).
steps.warn: A cracked or worn-out chain can break while running (STIHL MS 162/172).

steps.text: Find the shortest cutter and mark it with a felt pen: every cutter gets filed back to that length (STIHL UK sharpening).

Set the file in a file holder: file square to the side of the bar and level, unless your chain's chart says to tilt it down, the holder's angle line parallel to the chain at the angle for your chain (30° for most STIHL and the Husqvarna chains listed for the 450 II), with a fifth to a quarter of the file showing above the top plate (STIHL MS 162/172, Oregon M&S manual, STIHL UK sharpening, Husqvarna 450 II).

File from the inside of the cutter outward, on the forward stroke only, lifting the file on the way back. Two or three strokes are usually enough, taking only a little off each; count them and stop when the cutting edge is bright all along (STIHL MS 162/172, Oregon sharpening). Turn the file a little now and then so it wears evenly (STIHL MS 162/172).

File every cutter on one side with the same count, then turn the saw round and do the other side the same way. Finish with all cutters equal in length (STIHL MS 162/172, Husqvarna 450 II, Oregon M&S manual).
steps.warn: Uneven angles or cutter lengths make the saw run rough and raise kickback (STIHL MS 162/172).

steps.text: Every third or fourth sharpening, lay a depth-gauge tool for your pitch on the chain and file any depth gauge that sticks up through it flush with a flat file, then round its front edge. Never go below the tool (Husqvarna 450 II, Oregon M&S manual, USFS chain saw course ch3).
steps.warn: Depth gauges filed too low make kickback more likely and stronger. Don't file the bumper tie straps or bumper drive links on low-kickback chain (STIHL MS 162/172, Oregon M&S manual).

steps.text: Knock the burr off by running the cutters across a piece of hardwood, brush away the filings and oil the chain well (STIHL MS 162/172).

Fit the chain with the cutters on top of the bar pointing toward the nose (STIHL's arrows on the tie straps point to the tip). Turn the bar over each time you sharpen or change the chain (STIHL MS 162/172).

Tension it cold: bar nuts loose, lift the nose, take up slack until the chain sits against the underside of the bar (STIHL leaves a 1–2 mm (0.04–0.08 in) gap there) but still pulls round easily by hand, then tighten the nuts while still lifting the nose (STIHL MS 162/172, Husqvarna 450 II, Oregon M&S manual).
steps.warn: Wear gloves. A loose chain can jump off the bar (Husqvarna 450 II).

steps.text: Push the spark plug cap back on. Outdoors, with the brake on, start the saw on the ground with your toe in the rear handle, or with the rear handle held tight between your legs just above the knees; never drop-start it (STIHL MS 162/172, USFS chain saw course ch3). Then test the chain brake: brake on, full throttle for no more than 3 seconds; the chain must not move (STIHL MS 162/172). Husqvarna's test is different: at full throttle, tilt your left wrist against the front hand guard and the chain must stop at once, without letting go of the front handle (Husqvarna 450 II). Then check the chain throws a line of oil (STIHL MS 162/172, Husqvarna 450 II).
steps.warn: If the brake doesn't hold the chain, don't cut with the saw. Engine exhaust is carbon monoxide: never run a saw indoors (STIHL MS 162/172).

steps.text: After the first few minutes of cutting, stop the engine, brake on, and check the tension again: a warm chain stretches, a new one most. Oregon says to let the chain cool before you readjust it, and Oregon's corded-saw manual says never to tension a hot chain; STIHL allows taking up slack while it is warm (Oregon M&S manual, Oregon CS1500, STIHL MS 162/172).
steps.warn: A chain tightened hot and left tight shrinks as it cools. Oregon and the Forest Service say it can damage the bar and chain; STIHL says the drive shaft and bearings. Ease off a chain you tightened warm as soon as you stop.

steps.text: When you finish, with the engine off and the brake on, slacken the chain: STIHL says to release the tension after finishing work every time, because the chain contracts as it cools, and to tension it again before the next use (its battery-saw manual says two turns back on the adjuster) (STIHL MS 162/172, STIHL MSA 60/70).

notes:
## Why the chain matters
Kickback happens when the upper part of the bar nose touches wood or the chain is pinched: the bar is flung up and back toward you faster than you can react (STIHL MS 162/172, CCOHS kickback). Oregon lists eight chain faults that make kickback more likely or stronger: wrong sharpening angles, dull cutters, altered kickback-reducing features, depth gauges filed too low, wrongly shaped depth gauges, a loose chain, wrongly fitted parts, and loose rivets or cracked parts (Oregon M&S manual). Filing well is safety work, not just speed. Keep the bar's upper tip out of the cut too: CCOHS says not to cut in the kickback zone, and Husqvarna says not to let it touch anything (CCOHS kickback, Husqvarna 450 II). For cutting fallen trees safely see [Clearing a fallen tree](#guides/safety_clearing_blowdown); for the rest of the saw see [Chainsaw upkeep](#guides/repair_chainsaw).

A chain needs filing when it makes fine dust instead of chips, you have to push the saw into the wood, the cut smokes even with oil and correct tension, the saw pulls to one side, or it chatters (STIHL USA sharpening, Oregon sharpening). File little and often: Oregon suggests touching up at each refuel (Oregon sharpening, STIHL UK sharpening).

## The right file
The pitch is the chain's size. STIHL stamps a code on each depth gauge; Oregon prints a chain code on the drive links, and the chain box and the saw's manual give the file size (STIHL MS 162/172, Oregon sharpening). If you can't read any marking, measure from the centre of one rivet to the centre of the rivet after next and halve it (STIHL UK sharpening).

| STIHL code | Pitch | Round file (STIHL) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1/4 in | 4.0 mm |
| 2 | .325 in | 4.8 mm |
| 3 | 3/8 in | 5.2 mm |
| 4 | .404 in | 5.5 mm |
| 6 | 3/8 in Picco (low profile) | 4.0 mm |
| 7 | 1/4 in Picco | 3.2 mm |

Source: STIHL UK sharpening, STIHL MS 162/172. Husqvarna also lists 4.8 mm for its .325 in chains (Husqvarna 450 II). Use only saw-chain files: other round files have the wrong cut and give a badly filed chain (STIHL MS 162/172). The sizes in the table are STIHL's. The size follows the chain type, not only the pitch: Oregon's own pages give 7/32 in (5.5 mm) for several of its 3/8 in chains, 3/16 in (4.8 mm) for its 3/8 in Speed Guard, and 5/32 in (4.0 mm) for its 3/8 in low-profile chains (Oregon M&S 2004). Use the size on your chain's box or chart.

## Angles by chain type
- **Top-plate (filing) angle:** 30° for most STIHL chains; STIHL's Rapid Hexa is filed at 25° (STIHL UK sharpening). Husqvarna's table for the chains it fits to its 445/450 II gives a 30° filing angle for all of them (Husqvarna 450 II). Other chains differ. Oregon's own pages (2004 edition) give 25° for its 3/8 in Vanguard chain, with the file tilted 10° down; 35° for its 3/8 in S-70; and 30° for its 3/8 in low-profile XtraGuard (Oregon M&S 2004). Read the angle off the chain box, the maker's chart or the marks on the file guide, and keep the guide's angle line parallel to the chain (Oregon M&S manual).
- **Side-plate (cutting) angle:** Husqvarna lists the cutting angle, the file's position and the file's diameter as the things to get right when filing (Husqvarna 450 II). Hold the file square to the side of the bar and level unless the chain's chart says to tilt it, with a fifth (Oregon) to a quarter (STIHL) of its diameter above the top plate (Oregon M&S manual, STIHL USA sharpening, STIHL UK sharpening). Husqvarna's table gives cutting angles from 60° to 85° depending on the chain (Husqvarna 450 II). A felt-pen mark on the cutter face shows the problem: after two or three strokes the ink should be gone evenly; if not, the file is the wrong size or too high or low (STIHL UK sharpening).
- **Chrome:** the cutters are chrome-plated. If the chrome on a top or side plate is chipped, file back until the damage is gone, then bring the other cutters to match (Oregon M&S manual, USFS chain saw course ch3).

## Both sides equal
Cutters on one side point left and on the other side right. If one side is longer or filed at a different angle, the saw pulls sideways, runs rough, wears fast and kicks back harder (STIHL MS 162/172, STIHL USA sharpening). Count strokes, file the shortest cutter first and match the rest to it (STIHL UK sharpening). After several hand filings, the Forest Service guide says to have the chain ground on a chain grinder to restore the angles and even up the cutters (USFS chain saw course ch3).

## Depth gauges
The depth gauge (raker) is the hump in front of each cutter. The height difference between it and the cutter sets how thick a chip the cutter takes; every filing lowers the cutter, so the gauge slowly stands too high and the chain stops cutting (Husqvarna 450 II, STIHL MS 162/172).
- Check them every third (Husqvarna) or every three or four (Oregon) sharpenings with a depth-gauge tool for your pitch (Husqvarna 450 II, Oregon M&S manual).
- Typical settings: 0.65 mm (0.026 in) for STIHL 3/8 in Picco and for Husqvarna's .325 in chains; Oregon stamps the setting on many of its chains' gauges, for example .025 in (0.64 mm) (STIHL MS 162/172, Husqvarna 450 II, Oregon M&S manual).
- Too low is dangerous: kickback gets more likely and more violent. STIHL says a chain with gauges filed too low must be replaced or reground by a STIHL dealer (STIHL MS 162/172).

## When a chain is done
- STIHL cutters carry wear marks; when any mark has gone, replace the chain (STIHL MS 162/172).
- Husqvarna: replace it when the longest part of the cutting tooth is under 4 mm (0.16 in), when cutters are cracked, or when the chain is stiff (Husqvarna 450 II).
- Oregon: cracked or broken cutters, top plates or tie straps; bent, cracked or burned drive links; rivets loose enough to turn with your fingers (Oregon M&S 2004).
- Keep a spare: alternating two chains also spares the drive sprocket (STIHL MS 162/172). Store sharpened chains in oil (Oregon sharpening).

## Fitting and tension
The cutters along the top of the bar face the nose; STIHL's chains have arrows on the tie straps that point to the tip on top (STIHL MS 162/172). Chain, bar and sprocket must match in pitch and gauge (CCOHS kickback, Husqvarna 450 II).

| Maker | How tight |
|---|---|
| STIHL (MS 162/172) | 1–2 mm (0.04–0.08 in) gap between the bar's underside and the chain, still pulls easily by hand |
| Husqvarna (450 II) | Tight against the bar, pulls round freely, doesn't hang |
| Oregon, solid-nose bar | Lowest tie straps and cutters just touch the bottom of the bar rail |
| Oregon, sprocket-nose bar | Tighter: lowest tie straps and cutters touch the rail firmly |

Sources as named in the table (Oregon M&S manual). A chain stretches when it warms up, new chain most (STIHL MS 162/172). Oregon and the Forest Service say to adjust tension only once the chain has cooled, because a chain tightened hot shrinks onto the bar as it cools (Oregon M&S manual, USFS chain saw course ch3). STIHL allows taking up slack during work but says to slacken the chain after work every time (STIHL MS 162/172).

## The chain brake
The brake stops the chain when your left hand pushes the front hand guard forward, or by inertia in a hard kickback. It reduces the risk of injury but does not prevent kickback; nor do low-kickback chains and bars (STIHL MS 162/172, CCOHS kickback). STIHL marks its low-kickback chains and bars with green labels; they meet CSA Z62.3, and STIHL warns that chains built for faster cutting or easier sharpening are more prone to kickback (STIHL MS 162/172). Keep the low-kickback chain on a home saw.
- **Before work:** idle, brake on, full throttle for no more than 3 seconds: the chain must not turn (STIHL MS 162/172).
- **Inertia check (engine off):** hold the saw in both hands over a stump, let go of the front handle and let the bar nose drop onto the stump; the brake should snap on (Husqvarna 450 II).
- Wood dust, resin and dirt on the brake band and clutch drum weaken it: brush them clean (Husqvarna 450 II, CCOHS kickback). STIHL wants the brake inspected every 3 months in heavy use, 6 months part time and 12 months occasional (STIHL MS 162/172). With no dealer, a brake that slips in either test means the saw is parked.

## Gear
Leather gloves while filing (CCOHS chainsaw PPE says leather gloves can help prevent cuts when sharpening) and eye protection (Oregon sharpening). For cutting: helmet with face screen and ear muffs, safety glasses, cut-resistant chaps or trousers, gloves and chainsaw boots, as in [Clearing a fallen tree](#guides/safety_clearing_blowdown) (CCOHS chainsaw PPE). That guide also covers working with a partner, never alone.
